title: The City in a Speck
principle: That tiny city is called a cell.

t: What if a whole city had to fit inside something smaller than a grain of sand?
What if a whole city — power stations, walls, a library, delivery vans — had to fit inside something smaller than a grain of sand?
A city needs power, walls, instructions, transport and waste disposal. Now fit all of it into something you cannot see.
Every function a city performs, running continuously, inside a volume of about four picolitres. No pause for maintenance.
sub: It already happened. You are made of about thirty trillion of them.
It already happened, about four billion years ago. You are made of roughly thirty trillion of them.
This is not a metaphor for a cell. It is a fair description of one.
Roughly 3 × 10¹³ of them, in about 200 distinct types, in you right now.

question: How many of these tiny cities would fit across a full stop?
How many cells would fit across the full stop at the end of this sentence?
A typical human cell is about 20 micrometres across. How many fit across a 0.5 mm full stop?
Given a 20 µm cell and a 0.5 mm printed full stop, estimate the linear packing count.
note: Guessing is the point. Nobody knows this one until they check.
Commit to a guess before you look — a guess you have made is what makes the answer stick.
Estimate before checking. The gap between your estimate and the answer is what you will remember.
Order-of-magnitude estimation first. Anchoring on your own wrong estimate is what makes the correction memorable.

stages.label: How close are we?
captions: A whole city. You can see the buildings.
One street. You could walk down it.
A single brick. About as wide as your thumb.
A grain of sand. Now you need to squint.
A cell. You have run out of eyes — this needs a microscope.
t: Drag the slider. Watch how much smaller each step is.
Drag the slider. Each step is about ten times smaller than the last.
after: Every step shrank by ten. Five steps, and a city became a cell.
Five steps of ten. That is how you get from a city you can walk through to something you cannot see.

stages.label: Powers of ten
captions: 10⁻⁶ m — a mitochondrion, and a bacterium beside it
t: Move it. Work out where a cell sits before the label tells you.
Each step is one order of magnitude. Predict where a eukaryotic cell falls before you reach it.
after: A cell sits five orders of magnitude below you. Its power plants sit one below that — and they are the size of a whole bacterium, which is a clue we will come back to.
Five orders below a human, one further to the organelle. That a mitochondrion is bacterium-sized is not a coincidence; it is the evidence for endosymbiosis.

t: That tiny city is called a cell.
That tiny city has a name: a cell. It is the smallest thing that is properly alive.
A cell is the smallest unit that performs every function we call living — it takes in energy, keeps itself separate from its surroundings, and copies itself.
A cell is the smallest self-maintaining thermodynamic system: it imports free energy, holds a boundary against equilibrium, and reproduces its own organisation.
sub: Everything alive is made of them.
Everything alive is made of them — you, a mushroom, the mould on old bread.
Every living thing is one cell, or many. There is no third option.
No known life escapes this: unicellular or multicellular, with viruses sitting outside the definition precisely because they lack it.

t: Doctors look at your cells to find out why you feel poorly.
When a doctor takes a blood sample, they are counting and looking at cells. The shape of them says what is wrong.
A blood film is read cell by cell: shape, size and count identify anaemia, infection and leukaemia long before other symptoms are clear.
Cytology is diagnosis at the scale you just explored — morphology and count in a stained smear remain first-line for a large fraction of haematological disease.

q: Roughly how big is a typical human cell?
What is the approximate diameter of a typical human cell?
Order of magnitude for a typical eukaryotic cell diameter?
options: Too small to see without a microscope
About the size of a grain of sand
Big enough to see if you look closely
why: About 25 cells fit across a full stop. Your eyes stop working long before that.
About 25 fit across a full stop — roughly 20 micrometres each. The eye can just about resolve 100 micrometres, so a cell is about five times too small.
≈20 µm. Unaided visual acuity bottoms out around 100 µm, so a cell is about five times below the limit.
≈20 µm, against an unaided resolution limit near 100 µm — hence the entire history of the field waiting on lens grinding.

q: What makes a cell like a city?
Why is a cell more like a city than like a brick?
In what sense is a cell a system rather than a component?
Why does the city analogy hold and the brick analogy fail?
options: It has many parts, each doing a different job
It is made of one solid material
It is the same all the way through
why: A brick is the same all the way through. A cell has power, walls and instructions — all different, all working at once.
A brick is uniform. A cell has a boundary, power plants, an instruction store and transport, all running at the same time and depending on each other.
A brick is homogeneous and passive. A cell is compartmentalised and active: each organelle performs a distinct function, and removing one stops the whole.
The analogy holds on functional differentiation and interdependence — remove the power plant and the instruction store stops being read. A brick has neither property.
